title: Compound interest
body: With compound interest you earn interest on your savings and on the interest already added. Over many years this snowballs: money growing at 8% a year roughly doubles in 9 years and quadruples in 18.

title: Simple vs compound interest
body: Put 1,000 away at 10% a year for 2 years. Simple interest pays 100 each year: 1,200. Compound interest pays 100 in year one, then 10% of 1,100 (110) in year two: 1,210. The gap grows every year.

title: The rule of 72
body: To estimate how many years money takes to double, divide 72 by the yearly growth rate. At 6%, 72 ÷ 6 = 12 years. It also works for debt and inflation: at 12% inflation, prices double in about 6 years.

title: Diversification
body: Diversification means spreading money across different investments, such as different companies, sectors and types of asset, so one failure does not wipe you out. It reduces risk without necessarily reducing returns.

title: Inflation eats cash
body: If inflation is 8% and your savings earn 3%, your money buys about 5% less each year even though the number grows. What matters is the real return: your interest rate minus inflation.

title: Stocks and bonds
body: A stock (share) is a small piece of ownership in a company; its value rises and falls with the company. A bond is a loan you make to a company or government, which pays you interest and returns your money at the end.

title: Index funds
body: An index fund owns all the shares in a market index, such as the 500 companies in the S&P 500, instead of trying to pick winners. It offers wide diversification and usually low fees.

title: What APR tells you
body: The annual percentage rate (APR) shows the yearly cost of a loan, including interest and many fees, as a single percentage. Comparing APRs is a better way to compare loans than looking at monthly payments.

title: Credit scores
body: A credit score is a number lenders use to judge how likely you are to repay debt. Paying bills on time and not borrowing close to your limits tend to improve it. A better score usually means cheaper loans.

title: Your net worth
body: Net worth = what you own (assets) minus what you owe (liabilities). A house worth 50,000 with a 30,000 loan left adds 20,000 to your net worth. Tracking it once a year shows real progress.

title: Revenue is not profit
body: Revenue is all the money a business takes in from sales. Profit is what is left after paying all costs: stock, rent, wages, taxes and interest. A business can have high revenue and still make a loss.

title: Cash flow
body: Cash flow is the money moving in and out of a business or household over time. A profitable business can still fail if customers pay late and it cannot cover bills today. Watch the timing, not just the totals.

title: Dollar-cost averaging
body: Investing a fixed amount at regular times, for example every month, whatever the price. You automatically buy more when prices are low and less when they are high, and you avoid trying to time the market.

title: Risk and return
body: Investments that can earn more usually carry more risk of loss. Savings accounts are safe but grow slowly; shares can grow faster but can fall sharply. Be suspicious of anyone promising high returns with no risk.

title: How Ponzi schemes work
body: A Ponzi scheme pays earlier investors with money from new investors instead of real profits. It needs ever more new money, so it always collapses. Warning signs: guaranteed high returns and pressure to recruit others.

title: M-Pesa
body: M-Pesa, launched in Kenya in 2007 by Safaricom and Vodafone, lets people send, receive and store money using a basic mobile phone. It brought financial services to millions of people without bank accounts.

title: Dividends
body: A dividend is a share of a company's profit paid out to its shareholders, often every quarter or year. Not all companies pay them; some reinvest profits to grow instead.

title: The break-even point
body: Break-even is the level of sales where total income equals total costs, so there is no profit and no loss. Fixed costs ÷ (price − variable cost per unit) gives the number of units you must sell.

title: What collateral is
body: Collateral is an asset a borrower pledges to secure a loan, such as a house, car or land. If the loan is not repaid, the lender can take the collateral. Secured loans usually have lower interest rates.

title: Budgeting basics
body: A budget plans where your money goes before you spend it. List your income, then fixed costs (rent, transport), then savings, then flexible spending. Saving first, as soon as you are paid, makes it far more likely to happen.

title: Emergency savings
body: An emergency fund is money kept aside for surprises such as job loss or medical bills. A common guideline is 3 to 6 months of essential expenses, kept somewhere safe and easy to reach.

title: Good debt and bad debt
body: Borrowing to buy something that grows in value or raises your income, such as training or equipment for a business, can make sense. Borrowing at high interest for things that lose value quickly usually does not.

title: What an asset is
body: An asset is anything you own that has value or produces income: cash, land, a business, shares. A liability is something you owe: loans and unpaid bills. Building wealth means growing assets faster than liabilities.

title: Fees add up
body: A 2% yearly fee sounds small, but over 30 years it can take a large share of your investment growth, because the fee is charged on your whole balance every year. Always check the costs of any investment.

title: Finance word: equity
body: Meaning: ownership value, such as shares in a company, or the part of a house you own outright after the loan.
example_sentence: After ten years of payments, she had built up equity in her home.

title: Finance word: portfolio
body: Meaning: the collection of all the investments a person or organisation holds.
example_sentence: His portfolio includes shares, bonds and some land.

title: Finance word: overhead
body: Meaning: the ongoing costs of running a business that are not tied to a specific product, such as rent and electricity.
example_sentence: Working from home kept the startup's overhead low.

title: Finance word: principal
body: Meaning: the original amount of money borrowed or invested, not counting interest.
example_sentence: Each payment covers some interest and some of the principal.

title: Finance word: yield
body: Meaning: the income an investment produces, usually shown as a yearly percentage of its price.
example_sentence: The bond has a yield of 7% a year.

title: Finance word: default
body: Meaning: failing to repay a debt on time as agreed.
example_sentence: Missing three payments put the loan in default.

title: Interest on interest
body: Saving check.
statement: With compound interest you also earn interest on past interest
explanation: Interest is added to your balance and then earns interest itself. That is compounding.

title: Doubling money
body: Rule of 72.
statement: By the rule of 72, money growing at 6% a year doubles in about 12 years
explanation: 72 ÷ 6 = 12. The exact answer is about 11.9 years.

title: Simple interest
body: Interest check.
statement: 1,000 at 10% simple interest for 2 years grows to 1,210
explanation: Simple interest pays 10% of the original 1,000 each year: 100 + 100 = 200. 1,210 is the compound result.

title: Revenue and profit
body: Business check.
statement: Revenue and profit mean the same thing
correct_answer: No: profit is revenue minus costs
explanation: Revenue is all money from sales. Profit is what remains after paying every cost.

title: Spreading risk
body: Investing check.
statement: Diversifying means spreading money across different investments
explanation: Spreading money means one bad investment cannot sink everything.

title: Spot the scam
body: Fraud check.
statement: A Ponzi scheme pays old investors with money from new investors
explanation: There are no real profits, only new money moving to older investors, so it must collapse.

title: Measuring wealth
body: Personal finance check.
statement: Net worth is what you own minus what you owe
explanation: Assets minus liabilities equals net worth.

title: Cash and inflation
body: Saving check.
statement: Keeping all your savings in cash fully protects them from inflation
correct_answer: Inflation reduces what cash can buy
explanation: Cash keeps its number but loses buying power when prices rise.

title: What a bond is
body: Investing check.
statement: Buying a bond means lending money to a company or government
explanation: A bond is a loan. The issuer pays interest and returns the money at maturity.

title: Mobile money origins
body: Fintech check.
statement: M-Pesa mobile money was launched in Kenya
explanation: Safaricom and Vodafone launched M-Pesa in Kenya in 2007.

title: Beta and market risk
body: Beta measures how strongly a share moves with the market. A beta of 1.5 means it tends to move 1.5% when the market moves 1%. The capital asset pricing model (CAPM) says investors should expect higher returns for higher beta.

title: The efficient market hypothesis
body: If share prices already reflect all public information, consistently beating the market by picking shares is very hard. The evidence is debated, but most professional fund managers fail to beat their benchmark index over long periods.

title: Options: calls and puts
body: A call option gives the right, but not the obligation, to buy an asset at a set price by a set date; a put gives the right to sell. Farmers, miners and airlines use options and futures to lock in prices and reduce risk.

title: Leverage cuts both ways
body: Borrowing to invest magnifies results. Buy a 100,000 asset with 20,000 of your own money and 80,000 of debt: a 10% rise gives you a 50% gain, but a 20% fall wipes out your whole stake.
